questions.q: Why does searching Shodan for a target organization still count as passive reconnaissance?
options: Shodan already scanned the internet and indexed the results — you're querying its existing database, not probing the target yourself
Shodan requires written permission from the target before any search can run
Shodan only shows information about organizations that have gone out of business
Shodan encrypts all query traffic so the target can never detect it
questions.explain: Shodan performs the internet-wide scanning itself; a search against its index (e.g. org:"Target Company" port:22,3389) retrieves pre-existing data without a probe of your own ever reaching the target.

questions.q: What does running `theHarvester -d target-company.com -b all` actually do?
options: Launches an active exploit against every subdomain found
Deletes all publicly cached pages related to the target domain
Queries dozens of public OSINT sources in one pass and deduplicates the results into emails, subdomains, and names
Sends a phishing email to every address it discovers automatically
questions.explain: theHarvester automates OSINT collection across many sources at once (search engines, PGP key servers, CT logs, Shodan, and more) with the -b all flag, saving dozens of manual lookups.

questions.q: In Google dorking, what does the `filetype:pdf` operator help you find when combined with `site:target-company.com`?
options: The target's internal firewall rule set
Exposed documents on the target's domain, which often carry useful metadata like author names or software versions
A list of every employee's login password
The physical IP address of the target's headquarters
questions.explain: filetype:pdf scoped to the target's domain surfaces publicly indexed documents — policies, proposals, org charts — and document metadata can reveal authorship and tooling details.

questions.q: Why is `intitle:"index of"` a useful Google dork during OSINT?
options: It only works on sites hosted by Google itself
It reveals the target's DNS zone transfer records directly
It bypasses any login page automatically
It finds open directory listings that regularly expose files nobody intended to publish
questions.explain: "index of" is the literal title browsers show for an open directory listing, so this dork surfaces unintentionally exposed file listings crawled by Google.

questions.q: A pentester finds an employee's name on LinkedIn and uses it for a phishing simulation that the signed scope explicitly authorizes against that named role. Later, they also look up that employee's personal Instagram and family members out of curiosity. What's true here?
options: Both actions are fine, since LinkedIn and Instagram are both public
Neither action is OSINT, since social media is never a legitimate source
The LinkedIn lookup is legitimate, scoped OSINT; looking up personal accounts and family members beyond the authorized target list is a scope violation
Only the Instagram lookup is a problem; LinkedIn is always off-limits for OSINT
questions.explain: Authorization typically names specific employees or roles as social engineering targets. Going beyond that — personal accounts, family members, anyone not on the written list — is a scope violation even when the data is technically public.
